name: IoT Data Platform
description: Design an IoT data ingestion and analytics platform handling millions of device telemetry events. Covers MQTT ingestion, stream processing, time-series storage, and raw data archival.

learnSteps.title: Device Ingestion at Scale
learnSteps.description: Millions of IoT devices send telemetry (temperature, GPS, heartbeat) via MQTT or HTTP to the API Gateway. The gateway authenticates devices using mTLS certificates, validates payloads, and immediately publishes messages to Kafka. This decouples device-facing connectivity from downstream processing, preventing backpressure from slowing device communication.

learnSteps.title: Real-Time Stream Processing
learnSteps.description: Apache Flink consumes from Kafka and applies windowed aggregations (1-minute averages, anomaly detection, geofence checks). It enriches events with device metadata and routes processed results to downstream sinks. Flink's exactly-once semantics with Kafka ensure no data loss or duplication, even during worker failures.

learnSteps.title: Hot Path: Time-Series Analytics
learnSteps.description: Aggregated metrics are written to InfluxDB for real-time dashboards and alerting. InfluxDB's columnar storage and retention policies automatically downsample old data (e.g., 1-second resolution for 7 days, 1-minute for 90 days). Queries like 'average temperature over last hour for building-42' complete in milliseconds.

learnSteps.title: Cold Path: Raw Data Archival
learnSteps.description: Raw events are written to S3 in Parquet format partitioned by device ID and timestamp. This data lake serves batch analytics (Spark/Presto), ML model training, and regulatory compliance. S3 lifecycle policies transition data to cheaper tiers (Glacier) after 30 days. The hot/cold path split ensures real-time queries stay fast while all data remains accessible.

chaosScenarios.name: Device Reconnect Storm
chaosScenarios.description: A regional network outage heals and hundreds of thousands of devices reconnect to the MQTT broker simultaneously
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Connection-establishment rate spikes 50x; CONNACK latency climbs to seconds and the broker sheds connections. Devices buffer telemetry locally, then flush on reconnect — ingestion dips, then surges well above steady state into Kafka.
mitigationSteps: Enable connection rate limiting at the broker
Verify device firmware applies jittered exponential backoff
Scale broker nodes horizontally before the buffered-data flush wave
Watch CONNACK p99 and Kafka produce rate until both normalize

chaosScenarios.name: Stream Processor Crash and Checkpoint Restore
chaosScenarios.description: The Flink job crashes and restores from its last checkpoint, replaying a window of already-processed events
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Ingestion into Kafka continues unaffected — the durable buffer does its job. Downstream writes stop and consumer lag grows linearly. On restore, events since the last checkpoint are reprocessed; without idempotent sinks this writes duplicate points to InfluxDB.
mitigationSteps: Confirm automatic restart restored from the latest checkpoint
Verify InfluxDB writes are idempotent (same timestamp+tags upsert)
Track consumer lag drain rate; scale task managers if recovery is slow
Confirm Kafka retention comfortably covers the outage window

chaosScenarios.name: Time-Series DB Write Stall
chaosScenarios.description: InfluxDB compaction backlog saturates disk I/O and write requests start timing out
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Flink sink backpressure propagates upstream and Kafka consumer lag grows; dashboards go stale but no data is lost. The S3 archival path is unaffected and stays current.
mitigationSteps: Throttle dashboard query load to free I/O for compactions
Expand storage IOPS or add a write-capable node
Let Kafka absorb the backlog — verify retention headroom
Downsample or drop high-cardinality series contributing to compaction debt

bottleneckProgression.description: MQTT broker saturates on persistent connection and keepalive overhead from the device fleet
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale broker cluster horizontally, lengthen keepalive intervals, shard devices by region

bottleneckProgression.description: Flink parallelism saturates on payload decoding, enrichment, and windowed aggregation
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Increase job parallelism, add task managers, fix key skew from chatty devices

bottleneckProgression.description: InfluxDB write throughput hits the disk I/O ceiling; compactions fall behind
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Shard by device/tenant, batch writes into larger points, downsample at ingest

expectedIssues.title: Tag Cardinality Explosion
expectedIssues.description: Unbounded tag combinations (device ID x firmware x location) blow up the InfluxDB series index and memory
expectedIssues.mitigation: Tag schema governance, hard cardinality limits, keep high-cardinality identifiers as fields not tags

expectedIssues.title: Device Clock Skew and Late Events
expectedIssues.description: Devices with drifting clocks or buffered offline data deliver out-of-order events that corrupt windowed aggregations
expectedIssues.mitigation: Event-time processing with watermarks and bounded allowed-lateness; quarantine wildly skewed timestamps

expectedIssues.title: Malformed Firmware Payloads
expectedIssues.description: A bad firmware rollout emits malformed payloads that crash-loop the parse stage
expectedIssues.mitigation: Schema registry validation at ingest, dead-letter queue for unparseable events, per-firmware-version error metrics

expectedIssues.title: Consumer Outage Exceeds Kafka Retention
expectedIssues.description: If downstream processing stays down longer than topic retention, unconsumed telemetry is permanently lost
expectedIssues.mitigation: Size retention to 72h, enable tiered storage, alert when lag exceeds 50% of the retention window

expectedIssues.title: Chatty Device Partition Skew
expectedIssues.description: Partitioning by device ID lets a few misbehaving high-frequency devices skew load onto single partitions
expectedIssues.mitigation: Composite partition keys, per-device rate limiting at the broker, partition rebalance monitoring

steps: Confirm the Flink job is healthy and checkpointing
Check for skewed partitions from chatty devices
Scale task managers and verify lag is draining
Extend topic retention if drain will take longer than the remaining window
Verify device backoff config is active fleet-wide
Scale broker nodes ahead of the buffered-telemetry flush
Monitor CONNACK p99 and produce rate until stable
Check compaction queue and disk I/O saturation
Throttle dashboard queries to free I/O headroom
Add IOPS or a write node; let Kafka buffer meanwhile
Replay lagged data and verify no gaps in series

decisions.title: Kafka as the Durable Ingestion Buffer
decisions.context: Device telemetry arrives whether or not downstream systems are healthy; dropping it is unacceptable
decisions.decision: The MQTT broker writes everything into Kafka before any processing happens
consequences: Downstream outages cost latency, not data — within the retention window
Replayability enables reprocessing after parser bugs or schema changes
Topic retention sizing becomes the explicit data-loss boundary

decisions.title: Dual Sink: Hot Time-Series Path + Raw Archive
decisions.context: Dashboards need second-level freshness on aggregates; ML and audits need complete raw history
decisions.decision: Flink writes rollups to InfluxDB for dashboards and the untouched raw stream to S3
consequences: Raw S3 archive is the cheap, complete source of truth
InfluxDB stays small and fast by holding only hot, downsampled data
Reprocessing from raw data is always possible when requirements change

decisions.title: MQTT at the Edge Instead of HTTP
decisions.context: Constrained devices on flaky networks need small packets, persistent sessions, and delivery semantics
decisions.decision: Devices speak MQTT with QoS levels to a broker fleet acting as the ingestion gateway
consequences: Far lower per-message overhead than HTTP polling
Broker connection state becomes its own scaling dimension
Reconnect storms are a first-class failure mode to engineer for

tradeoffs.choice: Micro-batched writes to InfluxDB instead of per-event writes
tradeoffs.benefit: An order of magnitude fewer write operations and better compression
tradeoffs.cost: A few seconds of added dashboard latency

tradeoffs.choice: At-least-once delivery with idempotent sinks instead of end-to-end transactions
tradeoffs.benefit: Higher throughput and simpler operations than two-phase commit sinks
tradeoffs.cost: Sinks must tolerate duplicate writes (same timestamp+tags upsert)

alternatives.name: Direct Broker-to-Database Writes
alternatives.description: MQTT broker writes telemetry straight into InfluxDB without Kafka or Flink
alternatives.prosVsCons: Fewer moving parts and lower latency, but any database stall drops device data on the floor
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Durability under downstream failure is the core requirement; the buffer pays for itself in the first incident

alternatives.name: Generic Wide-Column Store for Telemetry
alternatives.description: Store time-series data in Cassandra with hand-rolled rollup jobs
alternatives.prosVsCons: Flexible and horizontally scalable, but manual downsampling, retention, and compression tuning
alternatives.whyNotChosen: A purpose-built TSDB ships compression, retention policies, and downsampling out of the box
